respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo81/1g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo81/1g.xml, deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Cette traduction couvre la dedicace, la theorie generale et l'equipement de la chasse, ainsi que la revue des animaux (chevaux, chiens, boeufs/taureaux, cerfs, chevres sauvages, elephants, rhinoceros, lions, lynx, l'onagre, le porc-epic, le tigre, l'autruche-chameau et le renard), soit environ la premiere moitie du texte grec conserve ; la suite (autres animaux et les techniques de chasse detaillees qui suivent) n'est pas encore traduite. Le decoupage en chapitres est une organisation thematique du traducteur (Claude), le texte grec source ne comportant pas de decoupage en chapitres numerotes coherent. Les courtes notices factuelles repetees et intercalees dans le texte grec source (formule recurrente sur des faits zoologiques/geographiques, sans lien avec le recit d'Eutecnius environnant) ont ete omises : elles semblent appartenir a une source de reference distincte melangee par erreur d'encodage au texte d'Eutecnius, et non a la paraphrase elle-meme.

div.head: Dedication to the Emperor and the invocation of Artemis
div.p: Oppian's books on the chase, I have transposed here for you, mightiest Caesar, out of the dark discordance of metre into the plain form of prose speech, a most excellent lesson in the art of hunting, so that, easily meeting with the book and gathering its fruit, you might be persuaded not to shrink from my labour. Nor did I look upon your own venerable and lovely wrestling-bout, O Oppian, master of wisdom, so celebrated for your famous song, without accomplishing it; rather, having finished, I have admired your beauty of speech.

To you do I dedicate these labours concerning the chase, most divine King Antoninus, the much-beloved light of the mightiest and most warlike of the Romans, the sweetest offspring of Severus and Domna — of Severus, the god of the Ausonians, of Domna, the most blessed of women, who obtained the noblest of husbands as her consort, and bore the fairest of sons; whom, were one to liken her to Aphrodite, or to name her the full-orbed Moon, one would not fail of the truth, and who might almost rival even the offspring of Zeus himself in the beauty of her children. But may the gods be gracious to you, O King, and above all Phaethon and Apollo.

You who, having received the kingship from a father who acquired it not without toil, as it were an inheritance, have set beneath your sceptres the whole earth, the whole sea, and all the rivers, whose beginning and origin are the streams of Ocean; and for you, of your power, time smiles brightly and is full of calm.

Indeed, I too set these hunting matters to song for you, not altogether without the god Artemis, the goddess of the chase — as though I seemed to hear her speaking. Rise up, and let us travel the difficult road of the hunt, hitherto untrodden by other poets; only, refrain entirely from those narratives that are hateful to me, and sing neither of the rites of Dionysus, nor of the triennial festivals, nor of the choruses of Asopus, nor of the voyage of the Argo, nor of the race of heroes, nor of battles, nor of the slaughters of Ares, nor of the loves of Aphrodite; but passing by all these, as matters hostile to my ear, relate the battles of beasts, the counsels of hunters.

When Artemis had said all this, I promised to do everything as she commanded. I hold, then, to the purpose set before me, and may it come to pass that I fail not of my hopes. But do you, O King, receive my discourse gently and kindly, stretching forth a hand that brings wealth both to the cities under your dominion and to those who write these matters of the chase.

div.head: The three kinds of hunting
div.p: Hunting is threefold for men, by favour of god: by air, by land, and by sea, though the same toil does not belong to all alike. For where is there an equal contest between catching a fish and a bird among the beasts of the mountains? Even if there is toil for the fowler in his hunting, yet pleasure is mingled with the toil, and he sets up his trophy over the creatures of the air without bloodshed. And if you consider the fisherman, you will see the same: he sits quietly upon a seaside rock, arming himself against the fish with rod and hooks, and before long the wretched creature, pierced through by the bronze, is dragged captive by the jaw, banished from its beloved haunt, and, though it thrashes to no purpose and dances about, it affords unspeakable delight to its captor. And truly for the fowler too the toil is sweet, as we have said; for he needs no sword or spear for his bird-hunting, since it is not only the eagle that attends him, but bird-lime and nets and reeds are brought to bear as well. Who, then, would dare to say that such sport is equal to the pursuits of hunting? Would one liken the eagle to the grim and fearsome lion? Who would compare the moray eel to the swift-swooping leopards? Let the wild goat be set beside the gull in the contest of the hunt,

nor the hedgehog beside the rhinoceros, nor the sea-monster beside the elephant. Great too is the difference in the skill of hand required of the hunters: those who occupy themselves with the chase overcome wolves, while the others master the tunny; and huntsmen have tamed wild sheep, while fowlers have mastered tame doves; bears are the prize of huntsmen, the sea-bream the catch of fishermen; the hands of horsemen are armed against tigers, those of fishcatchers against red mullet; trackers have mastered the boar, while the fowling kind have destroyed the nightingale. By as much, then, as the boar and the tiger, the bear and the lion, the rhinoceroses and the elephants, the wolves and the wild sheep are more valiant than doves and nightingales, than sea-bream and red mullet, by so much are the slayers of beasts nobler than those who labour about winged things and fish.

div.head: The equipment and season of the hunter
div.p: The hunt for men is threefold from the god: by air, by land, by sea; but let the Tritons and Nereus, the guardian spirits of the sea, follow along with my discourse, and likewise the swarm of nymphs who love birds; for it wishes to turn from these to the beast-slaying spirits, since there is need of their aid too for the matter in hand.

The young men who go out to the hunt — for from them my discourse must take its beginning — should neither be weighed down by excessive flesh, nor brought low by leanness; for bulk of body is ill-suited and slow for the pursuit of beasts, for leaping over ditches and crags, and useless besides for running, while leanness is treacherous in wrestling and grappling with wild animals.

The hunter, then, must avoid both extremes, and neither cherish the over-fat and over-fleshed body, nor the over-thin and fleshless one, but their bodies must be trained to a well-tempered mean, so that they may be light for running and strong for fighting.

Let the right hand carry two long javelins, and let a sickle hang fastened at the middle of the belt, that there may be means of defence both against beasts and against treacherous men. Let the left hand, for the man on foot, be free for the leading of the dogs, but for the horseman, for the handling of the bridle. Let the tunic too be gathered up and girded fast with a strap in place of a belt. And so that they may labour easily and pursue their hunting the more eagerly, let the cloak be thrown back from the shoulders, freed from both hands, as though releasing them from a bond and a hindrance; and those concerned with tracking should even have their feet bare of sandals, lest they wake the beasts by the noise. It is better still that they wear no tunic at all, so that the wind striking against it should not produce a sound and make the beasts, which are exceedingly timid of noise, take flight. Let this, then, be said concerning the equipment of hunters.

The season for hunting is not the same, but differs at different times: now at the beginning of day, now in the early evening; and indeed midday, and evening, and night too, when the moon shines bright, rouse the hunter to the chase. But for the more diligent of hunters every season and every day is fair and favourable for the hunt; spring above all, and autumn, when running is easier for horses and men and dogs alike; for just as spring is beginning, the air smiles, freed from the burden of clouds, the sea too is navigable for sailors, and the earth for plants

the rose sends up its bud gently from its calyx and unfolds outward. And as autumn wanes, the storehouse of the farmer flourishes with every fruit, the oil overflows the vessels that hold it, and the grape-cluster of the vine, crushed beneath tender feet, sets the wine-presses leaping, and the hives of the bees grow heavy with honey. Neither winter nor summer, moreover, is unprofitable or unsuited to the hunter who is not altogether sluggish and no lover of the chase; for even in winter the middle hours of the day yield good hunting to him who hunts, at which time the man overtaken in the woods by the sharp cold of the season is not overcome, but has found a remedy for what oppresses him: gathering brushwood, and then creeping beneath a hollow rock, and kindling a flame from the wood, he warmed himself and made his meal. So too is it fitting to do in summer, avoiding the fiery and wearisome heat of the sun, but going out to the hunt at early twilight, when the ox is led beneath the yoke and the plough is drawn to break up the earth, or else, if not then, toward sunset,

when the herds are driven together to the steadings, and the udders are full of milk, and the young, leaping from their pens, gambol about their mothers, each after its kind, calves about the heifers, lambs about the sheep, foals about the mares, and kids about the goats.

The complete hunters, moreover, ought to carry these weapons for the chase as well, differing indeed in their fashioning and in their names: I mean nets, cords, the all-catching net, snares, halters, nooses, and besides these those of iron — the javelin, the hunting-spear, the boar-spear, poles, and the arrow sent from the bow; yes, and double-edged knives, ox-goads, and the hare-slaying trident, and besides these the hooked staves and crooks, so called from the curve of their shape; and to these let there be added ropes and cords and woven foot-snares, knots and stakes, and the many-eyed nets.

Let us now, after what has been said, make mention of hunting horses. Male horses are better than females for men who hunt, because they are swifter in running and more enduring for the length of the toil, and because mares in heat, aroused by desire for the males, send forth a love-whinny, and stir up to flight the timid and fearful deer, gazelles, and hares.

Just as among men there is much difference in appearance, size, temperament, and race, so too shall we find it among horses; and I, though it is a hard thing to make distinction of the best amid so great a variety, am ready to name those that excel in all points. I say, then, that the first place among horses belongs to those bred from Tyrrhenia, the Sicilians, the Cretans, the Mazices, whose nurse is Achaea, the Cappadocians, the Moors, the Scythians, the Magnesians, those from Elis; and with these are reckoned the Armenians too; reckon with these also the Ionians, the Thracians, the Libyans, and those from the Troglodyte country.

div.head: The best breeds of horses and their form
div.p: This has been reckoned by the older breeders of horses and cattle to be the best conformation and shape of the horse: great in body, holding the head high, the lower jaw a little above the neck, gently drooping; broad and bright between the brows, shaking thick the crest of hair about the forehead; the eye black and fiery, the brow black, broad nostrils, a well-proportioned mouth, small ears; let the neck be gently curved, the chest broad, the back wide, the body long, the spine cleft beneath sleek haunches, and let it have a long tail with straight hair; let it be supported too by well-knit and muscular thighs, and let the lower parts of the legs be straight and long and rather slender, the limbs not overly fleshy, resembling those of deer, the fetlock upright, the hoof round, high, and strong beyond those of deer, the strongest of all. Such is the hunting horse our account has described, following the ancient judges of horses; after this image is the Tyrrhenian horse depicted, and no less the Cappadocian and the Armenian, and the one nurtured by Achaea. A wondrous thing, too, has been observed of Cappadocian horses: while they are young, their strength is somewhat lacking, but as they grow old they gain more and more in vigour, and their running becomes swifter. These are fearless in war and bold against beasts, and would go to meet even fearsome beasts as heavily-armed soldiers would.
To speak generally, every noble and courageous horse, when the trumpet sounds the call to war, pricks up its ear and looks about on every side, watching for the ambush,

gazing fixedly at bronze and iron; and it knows the time for war and the time for staying at home, nor is it ignorant of the signal for an ambush against the enemy. You might see it drawing near the walls of the enemy, fearing nothing when the moment of siege is at hand, and when the arms-mad youth fence their heads with light shields, adorned with bosses, so as to be able to ward off the missiles from the walls, when the ray of the sun, striking upon the bronze of the shields, sends forth from there a double flash, rising from the east and sinking toward the west. For the horse is by nature most skilled in understanding, equal even to the most graceful of men, and it recognizes its rider exactly, and, on seeing him, at once sends forth a whinny, as though smiling and rejoicing together with him; and if it should fall in battle, it perceives the misfortune... so that the marks of its nature might be obliterated by the smell; unknowingly, O gods, it wrought a terrible thing, and that hateful and abominable union was accomplished, such as we hear was formerly brought about in Thebes when Oedipus lay with his mother. When, then, after their union, they were stripped of those deceiving coverings, at first they looked upon one another askance, and then, rearing up

and snorting, they broke their bonds in disorder, and let forth a whinny most harsh and shrill, as though calling the gods to witness their drunken folly and cursing bitterly him who had led the bride to the wedding; and afterward, weeping as it were and leaping uncontrollably, they dashed their heads against the opposing rocks, and, their bones shattered, sank down leaning upon one another after their destruction. Such is the ancient tale that has been told of horses. The best of horses for swiftness of course and speed of foot are those pastured about Sicily and Lilybaeum and the three-necked peak of Etna, where the giant Enceladus, enemy of the gods, lies shut up as in a prison, belching forth fire from the hollows of Etna, so that one might say

he was gasping and vomiting forth aetherial whirlwinds. Swifter of foot than those of Sicily are those beyond the Euphrates, and those whose nurses are Armenia and Parthia. The Iberians, however, have surpassed even the Parthians in excellence of limb, to whose running I think one might compare the eagle, or the swift-winged hawk, or the dolphin itself gliding lightly over the deep. So great is the excess of speed in horses; but though they have such swiftness, they have obtained neither sufficient size, nor strength of body, nor boldness of soul, and their running, moreover, is neither lasting nor steady, nor covers many furlongs; and there are also horses fair to look upon, but weak in the hoof and splay-footed. The Moorish horse is good at running and enduring of toil; after this, the Libyan, long-distance-running and long-suffering; both of these are similar in appearance, except that

the horses of Libya, whose mother is Cyrene, are noble and exceedingly strong, and have in addition length of body, since they surpass their kind by an addition of ribs and stoutness, whence they are of massive and larger bodies, and are horses most enduring of the sun's flame and of thirst. Cretan and Tyrrhenian horses are both fine both in length of body and swiftness of foot. The Sicilians, however, are swifter of course than the Moors, and more spirited, bright of countenance and grey-eyed, and they can even face a roaring lion. For this reason, too, those concerned with the hunting of beasts

have made use of certain horses matched to certain beasts, and have observed that one is a match for another: against the spotted-footed deer they have set the blue-eyed horse, against the bear the grey one, and against the leopard the black one, and against the boars they have set in motion the one with a fiery-red coat, just as they have opposed to the grey-eyed lion the grey-eyed and bright-eyed horse. Of all horses the Nisaean is the most excellent,
surpassing in beauty and obedient to the bonds of bronze and easily led, a mount befitting a king, short-headed, of exceeding neck, and golden-haired.

There is also among hunting horses one spotted and dappled, which antiquity calls "oryx-horses" for two reasons, either from their mountain-nurture, or from their maddened love of the female; for the poets use the word "rush" of the uncontrolled dashing after the female. Of these oryx-horses there are two kinds: some are variegated only about the back and neck with long, overlapping rings, as one may see; others are marked with round circles, like those of leopards.

Nature so painted the first kind, but the markings of the second are the invention of men; for while they were still infants, they were marked all over with a soft branding-iron shaped into a circle, and thus were graced with an ornament wrought by hand. And there is nothing strange in men having contrived such things, when even a foal, still unborn and confined within its mother's flanks, unseen and untouched, they have shaped as they wished, and, colouring images of horses invisible in the workshop of the womb, have made them stand thus. For whenever the female is aroused to desire and, as it were, awaits the male as a passionate lover, then those who tend the horses, having marked out his whole body beforehand with variegated colours of different hues, and having painted him over for the splendour of his form, make him ready for the wedding. Seeing him, you would liken him to a hero wearing a crown and clothed in splendid garments, breathing forth perfume and hastening toward the bridal chamber, where

he may meet his bride; and indeed they do not let him loose upon his beloved too quickly, but hold him back as he hastens, kindling the fire of his desire the more; then, having whetted his mad passion for love, at last and with difficulty they let him mount. The mare, then, having thus taken into her eyes the image of so fair a mate and so full of blossom,

have released doves' chicks whenever they come together for mating, and from this, through the delight and pleasure of watching, they have brought forth young of many-coloured forms. And this device has proceeded even to the shaping of human beings, and the Laconian sculptors employ painting as an ally of their art: for the most radiant of youths in their prime, I mean Nireus, Narcissus and Hyacinthus, Castor and Polydeuces, and the fairest of the gods, Apollo and Dionysus — these, having most carefully fashioned in tablets,

and having modelled them with exactness, they set before their own wives when pregnant, who, receiving as it were an emanation from that beauty, brought forth children fair to look upon and distinguished. Concerning horses, then, enough has been said to sufficient purpose; from this point our discourse wishes to make mention of dogs, and to teach which dogs are good for hunting.

div.head: The best breeds of dogs
div.p: The dogs from Paeonia are good, and the Ausonian, the Carian, the Thracian, the Iberian; Arcadia too is a mother of noble dogs, and Argos itself, and Lacedaemon, and Tegea; nor is the land of the Sarmatians the worst at rearing whelps, nor the Celtic land; Crete too has its share of excellence in the breeding of dogs, and Magnesia, and
Amorgos, and Egypt has good dogs; and indeed the Locrian dog and the Molossian are both apt, and the Locrian is acknowledged to be grey-eyed.

If, then, you should wish to produce from two breeds of dogs a single mixed and hybrid kind, I shall not hesitate to tell you both the season and the manner of their mating: let their union take place in spring, when marriage is at its height for all creatures, and desire and passion, and when longing for the female is instilled the more into the hearts of the males, and the goddess of marriage departs neither from air nor sea, but even the viper itself, full of bitter venom, comes then to the shore to mate with the moray eel of the sea, and there is no race, save that of the sea, that does not come under the sway of Aphrodite and love of marriage. In spring doves too rage with love for doves, and horses for mares, and bulls for heifers,

then too the ram mounts the ewe, and the boar leaps upon the sow, and he-goats cover the she-goats; and why need I speak of the rest? For among men too, at that season, loves go dancing round about, and Aphrodite, common to all, going about everywhere, ordains the unions of the marriage-bed.
Such, then, is the season for the mating of dogs; as for the manner, it is the union of the breeds with one another —

Arcadian dogs, those of Elis, Paeonian and Cretan, Carian and Thracian, Tyrrhenian and Laconian; and the Sarmatian dog is no ill-omened bridegroom for the Iberian bride: thus would dogs best be joined together.

But as for dogs, different men have judged different breeds to hold the first place among hunting dogs; to us, however, in this uncertain diversity, this one seemed in some sort the most beautiful in form and shape:
the body long enough to be self-sufficient, the head light, well-eyed with dark-blue-coloured eyes, the mouth wide-gaping and sharp-toothed, short ears,

closely covered with thin skin, a long neck, a broad and strong chest; let it have the front legs shorter than the hind ones, the limbs straight and lean and long, broad shoulder-blades, curved ribs; let the loin, too, be fleshy, not fat, and let its tail be taut and rather long: such is the shape of the swift dog that is to pursue deer and hares.

There is also a valiant and warlike kind of dog, which has leapt even upon bulls and rushed against the boar, and has not shrunk even from the lion itself — that well-nourished and exceedingly large kind, snub-faced in appearance, with a fearsome brow, fiery and glittering eyes as though bright-eyed, a shaggy hide, a strong body, and otherwise high-spirited and most vigorous. But this kind, as I have said before,

is a match for savage beasts, and is far more readily an easy expeller of weaker creatures. Worst of dogs are the white and the black-skinned, unable to bear either the flame of the sun or the cold of winter; but those would fare best whose forms are made to resemble the beasts, I mean wolves and tigers and leopards and foxes,
and indeed also those whose colour is likened to Demeter's; for these excel most of all in running and in strength.
Never allow the puppies to draw at the tender udders of goats or the teats of sheep, or of domestic dogs, and never let them suck milk from there; for in this way they become slow of leg and

sluggish and feeble; but if indeed you put them to the teats of a lioness or a she-wolf, or to the milk of hinds and gazelles that nurse them, then you would make them strong and swift of foot, nothing inferior to those who bore them.

Puppies bear such names as "wind-footed," "swift-footed," "sharp-footed," and the like, so that, hearing these often, they may become accustomed to swiftness of running. Hunting dogs ought to have familiarity and friendship with horses and huntsmen from infancy, but should be taught to nourish enmity and anger toward beasts alone; and they should be taught also to unlearn barking, for this is not lawful for a hunting dog, which ought rather to prove a good tracker and scenter.

Know that tracking is of two kinds, that of men and that of dogs: for men have judged the unseen paths of hidden things from their eyes, but for dogs their nostrils have become messengers of what is unseen, since they possess a much keener sense. The most favourable hunting for trackers occurs at the very depth of the wintry season, when

the observation of tracks presents no toil to the eyes, being clearly marked now in the snow, now stamped exactly in the mud; but spring is hostile and unfriendly to those we have mentioned, since the earth nourishes grass and is covered with flowery coverings, and the meadows grow purple with blossoms, and, through the fragrant breath arising from the plants,

the scent of the beasts is scattered abroad into thin air, and does not lead the sense of smell to a more exact perception of what is sought; but the season of autumn is sweeter and more welcome to dogs, because the plants too wither and grow old, and the breath of the hidden creatures is exposed bare and uncovered, and is thus most easily perceived.

There is found, moreover, a breed among tracking dogs, small to look upon, but worth as much as the great. The whelps are a food of Britain; "Agassaei" is the name given to these whelps. In size they are like these little house-dogs, which greed and gluttony have made accustomed to be fed about tables and dinners, gaping wide for whatever falls from there,

shaggy-haired, fleshless, sluggish-eyed, round-bodied, firm of foot, armed with sharp claws and bearing close-set canine teeth in their mouths; the Agassaean dog, then, is good of nose and best at tracking, and is skilled at finding not only the trail upon the ground, but also at perceiving the scent that is borne upon the air.
And a certain one of the hunters, wishing to make trial of the dog, contrived some such thing as this: the hunter, coming before the city — a hare, whether living or

dead, being in his hands — goes forward, dragging it along the ground just as the creeping beasts do, and makes its trail not in a straight line, but winds it in crooked turns to right and left, concealing as far as possible any perception of what he is doing. When he has gone forward from

the city, having buried the hare in a pit, he sets off back again toward the town, and then lets the dog go to find the quarry; and the dog, tracking the scent of the hare most carefully, snuffling, agitated, at a loss, not knowing what to do, desiring the thing longed for, yet vexed at not overtaking what he seeks — you would say, seeing him, that he suffered the passion of a maiden newly experiencing the pangs of childbirth, pierced by the pains as by arrows, who, through the extremity of her distress, utterly forgets propriety and decorum; for she casts off the veil from her head

and lets loose her dishevelled locks, and, her tunic drawn back and her breasts exposed, pays no heed, but now goes out to the porch, now betakes herself to the chamber, driven about by her suffering, and now falls to the ground wailing
and scratching her rosy cheeks; something similar happens to the dog, who, pained by his excessive distress, leaves nothing unexplored, not a hillock, not a stone, not

a fence, not a road, not a tree, not a vine, until, having used the air as an interpreter of what is obscure, and being informed by it of the hidden thing, he stands at the very spot where the object of his search lies, and his perplexity ceases. You might see him then leaping and

whining for joy, and behaving as calves do about their mothers, running round about the place that guards what is hidden, and you could not lead him away from there, not even were you to use much force, until he has completed his contest and taken possession by sight of what he desires. And if you should ever set him upon hares not yet hunted, you might clearly perceive here too his skilfulness: he walks quietly

with light and noiseless steps, and runs beneath vine-rows and the thick tangle of stubble, hiding his body and, concealing himself, imitates a treacherous kid, which, having watched for the shepherd to fall asleep, creeps along quietly, and, using his slackness for its own mischief,

waits its moment; then, all at once, it leaps forth as an arrow from a bow, or as a hissing serpent which a reaper or a clod-turner has roused unwilling from its bed — with just such a rush does the dog too spring joyfully upon the beast; and should he happen upon the quarry just then, he first masters it with his claws, and then, taking the burden up in his mouth, carries it to the huntsman, worn out and exhausted. Such a thing as we see happening in summer, when a wagon is bringing the ears of corn home from the harvest field: those neighbouring in the fields, perceiving it, run up at once, and, standing round about, one labours at the wheel, another at

the axle, another takes hold of the brick-work, so that the oxen may have an easier time and be somehow relieved of the burden of carrying, until, having reached the farmstead, they loose them from the yoke and refresh the sweating cattle, and the ox-driver, relieved of his toil, rejoices; you see the same thing happen also with the dog: for when he brings that hare, the huntsman meets him rejoicing, and, raising both the hunter and his catch from the ground, gathers them into his own bosom.

Do you yourself, fairest of goddesses, Artemis, daughter of Zeus, sister of Apollo, golden-girdled virgin, guide for me the course of my discourse, and tell me who was the first of men and heroes to take up hunting, and, by your own hand, to bring this great pursuit to perfection.

div.head: The origin of hunting: the centaurs, Perseus, Castor, and Pollux
div.p: There is a high mountain called Pholoe, swept by the winds; about its foothills the centaurs first practised hunting; the centaurs were beast-mingled and strange to look upon, composed of unlike natures, human from the loins upward,

and fashioned as a horse from there down to the feet. Of all men, Perseus the son of Zeus, who is also said to have cut off the head of the Gorgon, first devised the hunt; but this hero showed something quite extraordinary in his hunting, foreign to the laws of the chase; for, lifted up by winged feet, as the myth would have it, he caught hares

from the hand, jackals, wild goats, gazelles, and antelopes, and he even mastered deer by swiftness and speed of foot. To hunt mounted on horseback, however, is the invention of Castor, who, casting a javelin at some of the wild animals, and riding down upon others on horseback, made it his own particular contest, hunting on horseback especially at the noontide hour

and in the meetings with beast-slayers at the narrow crossings of the roads. Polydeuces the Lacedaemonian was the first to set dogs upon beasts; and just as he was mightiest at boxing, destroying whoever came to grips with him among his opponents, so too with dogs he mastered the beasts that fell in his way. Such, then, were these men; but Meleager, son of Oeneus, was the first to master, in hand-to-hand combat,

the entangling snares and nets of the beasts, and Hippolytus was the first to bring down beasts with the bow. These, then, are the ancient leaders in the art of hunting; but in later times many have been captivated by this most keen passion; for there is no one once pierced by the goad of the chase who would ever willingly abandon it, but he will remain most eagerly attached to it, and cling to it as though held by unbreakable bonds. For as it is sweet to lie down amid the flowers of spring and share in gentle sleep, and as it is sweet in summer to run beneath some cave and improvise a couch upon the ground and rest in the shade,

how great is the delight, too, and the sweet-hearted pleasure for hunters to share a meal upon the mountains; how great the joy of gathering flowers and drawing cool, pure, and sweet water flowing from a cavernous rock with a gentle and pleasant murmur, and of soothing the weariness of the hunt by bathing in that water; but what pleasure of goatherds' sweetness compares to the gifts of rustic folk and shepherds, brought to hunters in baskets?

div.head: The bull, its fights, and its regional varieties
div.p: But enough of this; let our discourse now take up the contentious and jealous nature of bulls concerning their mates. The greatest and best of the herd, superior to the lesser bulls,

sets himself up as self-appointed tyrant over the females as well; the males, therefore, shudder at him and cower before him as their lord, and the females as a harsh and savage mate, and indeed they are gripped by trembling and shrink back; yet his supremacy over his fellows is not long-lasting nor secure; for another bull, having gained the mastery elsewhere,

himself too, separating from his own herd, sets himself up for battle against the leader of the other herd. Both, then, boiling with rage, their eyes shooting fire and their breath breathing fire, pawing the ground with their feet and bellowing loudly, dash horn against horn and, in shocks of colliding foreheads, wound their bodies without mercy. Such a thing as triremes do too, at the time of a sea-battle, waging war beneath the waves; for there too two, standing out above the others, gleaming with the armour of their fighters, driven on by wind and oars, dash together prow against prow, and the din of men arises from the bronze, and the ships, torn apart and shattered, are scattered over the sea, and the whole sea seems to be constrained and burdened; just so, when

the bulls come together for battle, the crash of horns strikes up to heaven as they strike and are struck in turn, until one shall prevail over the other. But the one who has suffered defeat, seized by shame, runs off into the thick shelter of the woods, groaning at his misfortune and grieving, and, having spent a long time there quite alone, strengthening himself with more abundant food, and having trained himself for a second contest,

when he perceives that he is in good condition of strength, he bellows aloud like a great war-trumpet, and at once the woodland echoes back, giving answer to each cry; then, filled with boldness from his own bellowing, he comes down from the mountain and goes to meet his rival, and, clashing with him, more easily puts him to flight, having so nourished his body to nobility and abstained, through the cutting-off of lechery, from a strength that undermines it.

You would find that the shapes and characters of bulls differ. The Egyptian bull, for instance, is white in colour, exceeding in size, presenting to onlookers the appearance of a great cargo-ship travelling upon the land; gentle to men and tame, and readily yielding and submitting to whatever they incline it toward.

The Phrygian bull is tawny in colour, deep beneath the neck, the upper parts of its body resembling a sphere, its head raised on high, and strange in the nature of its high-standing horns; for these are not fixed firmly upon its head and rooted there, but move about this way and that and turn round.
Boeotia too bears spotted and one-horned bulls, and indeed one-hoofed ones; their horn, rising up from the forehead, is split from a single root into two branches,
and then, bending, turns to right and left, and, sharpening toward its tips, thrusts forward its points like spearheads.
All those who boast Pella and the Chersonese as their mother possess every virtue befitting a bull, being fiery and strong and great of soul, firm of horn, broad

and fleshy all over and fat, yet neither lean of body nor altogether wanting in flesh, but, avoiding the excess of both extremes, tempered to a mean, so that they are swift in running and vigorous in strength. Such, they say, were those which Heracles brought back, having earlier accomplished his labour by slaying Geryon at Erytheia, when he was also to accomplish a task for Archippus, ruler of Pella — for Archippus was indeed his friend and companion — no less honourable than those which Eurystheus, lord of Argos, imposed on him in his anger
at Hera's bidding. For the river Orontes, which flows past the lake of Antioch, being further inflamed and drunk with love for the nymph — Meliboea was the nymph's name, Ocean

her father — forgot his course to the sea, and flooded about the mountains and plains, now the mountain called Emblonus, submerging its foothills, now turning aside toward the land and covering it with his current, and sometimes
dragging himself along midway between Emblonus and Diocleia, which slope toward each other from east and west, and, behaving every way on account of his beloved, swelling and

roaring and drawing near the walls, and flooding with his water my own city, shaped as it is into a peninsula. So then, the river having thus gone mad for the marshy stream, Heracles brought about a separation of the waters with his strong arms, and taught the ill-fated lover to be temperate and not to love beyond his bounds, but that it is the law for rivers to mingle with the sea, and not to burden the fruit-bearing earth,

a strange thing indeed; and so, having cut through the steep crown of the mountains and drawn the river along as though by stony bonds, he straightened its course and persuaded it to journey toward the sea with a fearsome bellowing and an irresistible leap. Nothing compares to that sound and the violence of that rush, not even the raging waters of two opposing rivers pouring together into the sea, I mean the Scythian Ister and the Libyan Aegyptus, which, cutting off the northern ridge as it were with reins, and set free to unrestrained motion, are swept down from the heights and precipices and fall into the sea with a great crying out. So Orontes, violently cut off from his beloved and driven toward the sea, bellowed and groaned monstrously and terribly; and the earth, shaking off its burden and breathing again, became fertile

and fruitful, and yielded increase for the bearing of crops, and still bears its ears of grain and is heavy with its own growth, Heracles having thus laboured on its behalf. There too was Memnon, son of Dawn, whom
Achilles slew in battle; the Assyrians, then, mourn his death, and honour him as a god,
even in his death. But we have set before ourselves an encomium of our fatherland; let us, then, deferring the fuller praises of it to another occasion, hold to the matters before us.
In the Bistonian land of Thrace there is a race of murderous and irresistible bulls, called "bisons"
after the land that bears them; and they have this form: they carry a bristling mane upon shoulder and neck, and shaggy hair upon the jaw, distinguished in appearance,

tawny-maned, grim-eyed, such that one might call them lions reigning among beasts; and about the curves of their horns they present sharp points very like the barbs of hooks; their horns, however, do not bend toward one another in a sideways inclination, as we see most bulls do, but tend backward, curving upward and aloft, and if any beast or man should happen to be pierced by them, he is at once lifted aloft into the air. Their tongue is rough and narrow,
preserving the likeness of an iron file, with which, tearing the flesh, they lick it up.

That aforesaid land, however, is not good for bearing bulls, but it was, it seems, no poor nurse of deer. Well-antlered are these deer, distinguished, having large eyes, spotted and dappled on the back, river-crossing and high-headed, and otherwise stout and fat, save that they are slender in the legs and neck and scanty in the tail;

their nostrils are four-fold among creatures, opening two passages on each side for their breathing; their spirit is ignoble and feeble, their horns weak and powerless, and they are worst at warding off beasts and driving away hostile dogs, and are not even able to put to flight the cowardly hare.

These too, however, feel greatly the burning passion for love and desire for the female; they grow angry, indeed, like fighting cocks or birds. They have passages for their seed hidden within the belly along the flanks, which, if one should cut off, would at once turn a male stag into a female, and would strip its head of its horns, which would suddenly fall away. As for marriage, deer have a strange and unaccustomed law, foreign to that of other beasts; for they do not mate standing still in the woodland dells nor reclining among the flowers,

but pursuing the female as she runs, overtaking her in the run, and pursuing her as she tries to flee, he embraces his beloved, as it were, with his fore feet, while with the others he keeps pace with her uncontrolled running and does not let go, until he has accomplished the union. The female, however, when she must give birth, avoids the road frequented by men, and slips beneath the thicket that affords her safety.

div.head: The horns of the stag; the amphibious deer that cross the sea
div.p: To male deer their horn is an ornament and a glory; they take pride in it, indeed, and are made proud by it, and, when in time it falls to the ground, they bury it and hide it, that no one who finds it should take it up and enjoy their splendour; and they, ashamed to appear to their own kind bare of head and unadorned, hide themselves in the thick coverts of bushes.
There is also an amphibious kind, treading the land and cutting through the sea, sailing a self-conducted voyage; for when they must swim across the open sea, one leads the way,
and the rest all hold on, each leaning upon the one before, and thus in a row they set out on their journey across the sea. When the leader grows weary and gives out, another

takes over the leadership, while he, withdrawing to the rear of the column, and leaning upon another, rests a little from his toil; so too does that one, and again another and yet another, so that the toil and the rest are shared equally among all; and using their feet as though they were oars, by which the density of the waters is cleft for them, they hold their antlers high like sails, and, entrusting themselves to the winds for a fair passage, thus complete their crossing.

That deer are enemies of serpents, and serpents of deer, is made clear from what shall now be told: a deer, coming upon a serpent's lair in the mountains, and perceiving that its enemy dwells within, fits its nostrils exactly and closely to the mouth of the den, and, with a violent panting and a drawing breath, draws the hidden creature out and does not

leave off until it has drawn it forth, though it be unwilling; and the deer, torn from its beloved haunt and beholding the enemy, raised itself up erect, snapped its jaws, and displayed sharp and venomous teeth beneath its gaping mouth, with a terrifying hiss; but the deer, reckoning these things as nothing, as the terrors of an ignoble creature, remained calm, and, smiling as it were, laid hold of the serpent, and crushed with its mouth the creature that coiled about its feet to no purpose; you might see the wretched remains scattered upon the ground, twitching and trying to rise again, and falling once more to the ground for lack of the power to do so. And, seeing it, you would pity the sufferer for its being cut up in so many pieces. Thus, then, the deer showed itself the enemy of the serpent.

Consider, however, the opposite too: the far parts of Libya nourish a great multitude of these destructive creatures; watching, then, for whenever the sand holds a deer lying alone, many serpents creep up from every side against the one, and, surrounding it, then

fastening themselves upon it in its very mouth, saw through one limb after another with their teeth. And the deer, perceiving the pains, first rises to flee, trusting its safety to its feet, but, being helpless and unable to accomplish anything, stands still, oppressed by necessity, and, turning about, deals out its defence,

tearing at them. But though thus being bitterly destroyed, those serpents let go not at all, so fearless is their spirit and so full of shamelessness; and most of them, even while being trampled underfoot, are destroyed, and the ground bears some of their limbs half-eaten, yet still living and leaping about, while others, clinging fast to the very skin of the flanks

of the hateful flesh, hang half-torn, and, even dying, do not let go their hold upon the skin. The one thus suffering, at a loss on every side, compounds for himself a natural and untutored remedy: coming upon a river, and gathering crabs from there, and eating his fill of them, he has found a self-taught cure for what oppresses him,

so that the wounds from the bites close up and heal, and whatever remains fastened in his flesh by its teeth falls at once of itself to the ground. The deer, then, is long-lived and of many years; for this reason the ancient saying has repeated of it that it lives four generations of crows.
There is another kind of deer, called by men "broad-antlered";
the name itself declares its nature, for its horn rises up broad and spreading above its head.

There are also certain deer called "roe-deer," which the thick and shady covert of the woodland nurtures, otherwise exactly like deer, but having a hide marked with close-set spots, such as we see on the coats of leopards.

What has been said concerning deer is enough; let the discourse now pass on to the buffalo. This creature is smaller than the broad-antlered deer, but greater and taller than the roe; bright-eyed, fair and lovely to look upon; its horn-branches, from the head, are straight and stretched forward for some distance, and thereafter, bending, incline back toward the animal's own back. It has an exceptional love for
its dwelling and its bed and its accustomed haunts, so much so that if ever it is caught in snares and carried off by hunters to another place, provided only it should seize its freedom,

even if it should happen to be far from what it loves, it returns most gladly and with great ease to its familiar haunts, unable to bear wandering and being worn out as a stranger among strangers. It was not, then, only to men that their fatherland was dear and beloved, but into beasts themselves a keen longing for their own has been instilled.
The nature of the gazelle is plain to all, how they possess strength

and remain grazing together, familiar with one another, sharing the same lair; but they learned before long the disadvantage of this fellowship, and reaped a bitter harvest of their intimacy, becoming, instead of friends and companions, enemies and plotters against one another; for, through the cunning devices of hunters, gazelles were captured, deceived by false images of gazelles, and gazelles

There is also, in the mountains, a wild kind of goats and of sheep, not much larger in size than these domestic ones familiar to us, but very swift in running and strong to fight with their horns. Often, indeed, having charged even against a raging boar, it has matched the strength of its forehead against him and, prevailing, has dashed him to the ground. At other times

these creatures come to grips with one another in strife, and, when they clash, a terrible crashing of horns results, nor does the conflict cease on either side until one has prevailed over the other, and the one falls dead while the other bears off the victory. This too is a peculiar mark of wild goats: they have a hollow passage, like a pipe;

this is a channel for breathing; the passage extends from the teeth into the middle of the horns, and, opening out from there, discharges into the heart, and sends the breath directly to the lung. This is plain to see: for if one were to pour wax around the animal's horns, death follows immediately, since the passages of respiration are blocked and the breath is stopped up within.
This race is affectionate to an extreme degree: the mother

div.head: The onager and its jealousy
div.p: It is not seemly, either, to pass over the onager in silence, as though excellence were not proper to wild creatures; for it is to be seen broad and very great, bright in colour, firm in the fetlocks,
strong in the hooves, long-eared, and swiftest of all in running; nature has marked it around the middle of its back with a black stripe, black lines running along either side.
Its food is grass and the herbage that is the earth's blossom, and it in turn becomes food for the stronger of beasts, growing bulky and fat through its abundant grazing on plants.
A most sharp goad of jealousy pricks these beasts too, inasmuch as the male, being mad with love for many females, and suspecting theft of his marriages and fearing a treacherous adulterer,

nourishes a jealous passion, so that you would never see him apart from his mates, but he drags them along with him everywhere he goes, to pasture, to springs, to every outing. To such a pitch has jealousy inflamed the onager, that it extends its evil even to his own offspring; for when the female is about to give birth, that fearsome creature, sitting close by, watches the birth with a fixed gaze, and if a female should slip from the womb, he receives it and greets it, but if, on the contrary, a male, he grows savage
and furious, and rushes to bite off the young one's genitals with his mouth, lest, having come to maturity, it should some day wrong him in his marriages. The mother's heart is torn

and she labours for her child, but she has no power to defend her offspring, on account of the weakness and exhaustion of childbirth. Something similar happens among men too, in time of war, when mothers, embracing their children, suffer them, wretched women, to be slain and mangled by the hands of barbarians,

tearing at their cheeks, uttering groans and loud lamentation, unable to bend the murderer's will, but themselves too carried off, captives, into slavery: something like this the female onager seems to suffer for her child. She seems, indeed, to go about the young one as a suppliant, and to speak such words as these to her mate: "why have you changed your face,
husband, into something so harsh and grim, and why is that once bright and lovely countenance now stained with blood and grown savage? It is no face of a Gorgon that you look upon,

no lion's cub, no offspring of a she-dragon. You are tearing apart the child longed for by us both, the shared and thrice-desired offspring of you and of wretched me, cutting away with your mouth the parts that would have made him a father, and robbing him, born male by nature, of the very name of male. What have you done? Stop! You have accomplished an unholy deed, you have maimed the child's whole body, depriving him of what is necessary. Wretched are we both, child, you and I, in sharing this misfortune: for me the birth was untimely and my labour-pains in vain, and for you it is heavier than death to have come forth into the light, not torn apart by a lion's claws, but cut off by the murderous mouth of a father who hates his own child." Such words might one imagine her to speak; but that fearsome and implacable beast, unmoved toward gentleness, passes that impious and unlawful meal without pity through his mouth. So great, then, is the savagery of jealousy, which I, for my part, would say has the strength of fire and the hardness of adamant.
It has, then, disregarded natural kinship, spared not its own children, and waged war and enmity even against demigods, as Athamas and Theseus bear witness, and Philomela too, and Procne,
Themisto and Medea. It was jealousy, too, that set before Thyestes that unspeakable table, and made him, like a flesh-devouring beast, taste of his own children.

div.head: The wolf and the hyena; the lion
div.p: But do you consider for me also the wolf and the hyena: the one uncontrolled in the raging madness of its belly, a snatcher of kids and lambs, a secret plotter against the flocks; the other, a night-wanderer
itself too, making darkness a cover for its wrongdoing, and in this like the wolf

toward the dogs that busy themselves about shepherds and flocks; and it has a curved spine and thick hair, a narrow back and tail, its body marked all over with close-set dark rings. Certain of the ancients say that there is something in the hides of these creatures that instils fear and terror together; for if you should flay the hide of a hyena and make it into sandals for your own feet,

you would never fear the threats of dogs, but would silence their bold barking, and they would at once shudder and shrink back, perceiving you walking in such footwear. Likewise, too, if you should make a drum from the hide of a wolf, it would be far more resonant; and if other drums happened to be brought to that same place,
made from the hides of sheep, however hard you should strike them, they would remain silent, and what was once loud-sounding and vocal becomes then mute and voiceless.

I have also heard another thing worthy of wonder and of telling: that the hyena changes from female to male and back again from male to female, and does not remain the same in nature within the same year,
but now is known as bridegroom and father, now is seen as mother and one who has given birth.

There were once, it seems, wolves of many forms and many colours; the shrewdness of hunters has distinguished five kinds of these. And the one they have called the "archer": its form is tawny, its limbs rounded, its legs quick-moving, its belly white, its head exceptional,
its voice terrifying, its onrush swift, and it always shakes its head and has a fiery gaze.

From this, indeed, it also has the name "hawk" and "snatcher." It sets out at early twilight for its hunting, at the very break of dawn, with a great rushing sound, on account of its extreme voracity.

Its tail and flanks flash with the whiteness of its colour; it makes its dwelling, however, in the highest of the mountains, and when these are covered with snow in the season of winter, it comes down into the town, and, drawing near secretly, remains quiet and still, until it has caught something for its raging belly.

Now I must speak also of the tiger, which nature, I think, has fashioned among creatures as an ornament and adornment of beasts. So exceedingly beautiful and charming is this creature among wild beasts, as the peacock is among birds. In all other respects it is exactly like a lioness, save that its hide alone is many-coloured and variegated in a flower-dyed beauty
and gleaming with purple. Fiery is its eye, flashing with a shining brilliance; its body is strong and well-fleshed, its tail long, its face radiant,
its brow lowering, its teeth white and most pure, the swiftness of its legs exceeding, comparable even to the west wind itself, which many have called the begetter of the tiger,
falsely proclaiming that there is no male tiger, but that all are female, and share the bed of no male. But this account is false; for neither air

nor wind could ever be a bridegroom or the conductor of a bride. You may often see the male too, and admire him for his beauty and splendour; but because he is not easily caught in snares, fleeing hunters and hunting-gear, he goes forward into groves and mountains and leaves the female alone with her cubs, giving occasion to some thoughtless persons to suppose that the race is altogether without a male, while the female, left alone and grieved on her mate's account, made as it were blind by her suffering, easily falls into the nets and becomes a delightful catch for hunters.
The porcupines are fearsome and formidable beasts, wolf-sized, strong in body, rough in their bristling hair, just as nature has fashioned hedgehogs too.

Whenever, then, they perceive themselves pursued by beasts, they contrive the following: bristling their quills backward, they thrust them forward upright like arrows, and, defending themselves with these against their pursuers, escape the harm coming from them. Sometimes, too, they have made a hostile dog appear dead; seeing it, you would say that they defended themselves against their adversary by sending forth missiles as if from a bow. But hunters, knowing this, hold back their dogs and do not let them loose upon them, and contrive a stratagem instead, which I shall relate presently, as I describe the destructive plots of hunters against beasts.

We say some such things also concerning the fox; for its character too has much guile in it, and it prepares destruction for beasts and birds alike, and stealthily draws them in with its eye. Already, too,

it has exposed the vain devices of hunters through its watchful cunning; for it does not open its den with a single hole, but with many, at no small distance from one another, so that if snares and nets should be set about one entrance, it might not be caught there, but might have the other passages sufficient for its escape.

There is to be seen also a winged creature, two-natured and composite, the camel that is among ostriches, in the form of a four-footed creature and yet with the plumage of a creature of the air. Bird-lime does not catch it, nor snares

and reeds, as with the ostrich, but it has become a contest for horses and hounds, and a catch for unbreakable bonds; hence it too has been received into our memory as a prize for hunters, and is no discordant subject in the account of hunting that we are composing. In size it is such that it could carry a newly-grown child upon its shoulders, its legs are high, resembling those of camels, and roughened up to the knee with hard skin,
its head small upon an exceptional and smooth-feathered neck; it makes its flight not against the blowing wind, for fear of being wearied and weighed down by struggling against the contrary breeze,

but when the south wind blows, it hastens with the rushing of its wings toward the north, and when the north wind blows sharply, toward the south in turn, and likewise from the west wind toward the east, and from the east toward the west. Yet, though it cuts through the air swiftly with its wing, it lacks not swiftness of foot either,

but is able to cross the ground too with the lightness of its legs and the swiftness of its leap. Its mating with its mate, however, is not according to the custom of birds, for the male does not mount the female as is usual, but effects the union from behind and turned away, as
the camels among the Bactrians do. The egg that it lays is so great in size that it seems like a stone
